issues.legal_issue: A bona fide third-party purchaser’s rights in property acquired at a confirmed public auction cannot be displaced merely because of disputes between the original parties or later changes in the property’s value, absent fraud or collusion.
material_facts: The property was sold at a publicly advertised recovery auction, and the purchaser was the highest bidder.
The Recovery Officer confirmed the sale in the purchaser’s favour, and possession was delivered to him.
The purchaser was a stranger to the debt recovery proceedings and there was no allegation or proof that he had acted fraudulently or in collusion.
The High Court set aside the sale to work out equities between the debtor’s brother and the Bank, relying in part on the later increase in the property’s value.
issues.conclusion: The High Court could not set aside the confirmed auction sale on those grounds. The purchaser’s rights were confirmed, and his appeal was allowed.
issues.legal_principle: A stranger who purchases property bona fide for value at a court or recovery auction is treated differently from a decree-holder purchaser, and protection of such purchasers supports fair market prices at auction. Once an auction sale requiring confirmation has been confirmed, the purchaser’s rights accrue and cannot be extinguished except in exceptional cases such as fraud or collusion. The Court relied on Ashwin S. Mehta v. Custodian, Janatha Textiles v. Tax Recovery Officer, Nawab Zain-ul-Abdin Khan v. Mohd. Asghar Ali Khan, Janak Raj v. Gurdial Singh, Gurjoginder Singh v. Jaswant Kaur, Padanathil Ruqmini Amma v. P.K. Abdulla, and Velji Khimji and Company v. Official Liquidator of Hindustan Nitro Product (Gujarat) Limited.

predicates.challenge_to_confirmed_public_auction_sa: A party seeks to undo a property sale made at a public auction in a recovery proceeding after the sale has been confirmed.
predicates.bona_fide_stranger_purchaser: A purchaser who was not a party to the underlying dispute acquired the property bona fide for value at the auction.
predicates.no_fraud_or_collusion: No fraud or collusion in the purchaser’s acquisition of the property was alleged or established.

issues.definition: When a challenge concerns a confirmed public auction sale to a bona fide outsider and there was no fraud or collusion, the purchaser’s rights remain protected.

issues.legal_issue: A belated challenge to a recovery sale is not a basis for disturbing the sale where the challenger’s asserted ownership is unsupported, the challenger abandoned the recovery objection, an appeal was available, and third-party rights arose before the challenge was brought.
material_facts: The challenger relied on an unregistered agreement to sell made with his brother, who was one of the judgment-debtors; the Court held that the agreement did not vest a legal right in the challenger.
Although the challenger filed an objection before the Recovery Officer, he stopped appearing or being represented after October 2005, and the sale order was made more than two years later.
The challenger did not object to the attachment or the auction notices and did not object in the purchaser’s mutation proceedings.

A statutory appeal to the Tribunal was available against the Recovery Officer’s order, but the challenger instead brought a writ petition after the auction had been confirmed, possession delivered, and mutation completed.
The challenger’s writ petition was brought after third-party rights had arisen in the property.
issues.conclusion: The challenger’s objections and belated challenge should have been rejected for lack of a legal right, abandonment, and delay and laches; the High Court should not have disturbed the auction sale.
issues.legal_principle: An unregistered agreement to sell does not vest the asserted legal right in the property. Under Section 30 of the Recovery of Debts Due to Banks and Financial Institutions Act, a person aggrieved by a Recovery Officer’s order may appeal to the Tribunal; the availability of that remedy weighed against intervention in writ jurisdiction. A claimant who abandons an objection, does not challenge the attachment or sale notices, and waits until third-party rights have arisen may have the challenge rejected for delay and laches. No earlier case was relied on for this issue.

rule.if: challenge_to_recovery_sale and unregistered_agreement_claim and abandoned_recovery_objection and available_appeal_bypassed and delayed_challenge_after_third_party_rights

predicates.challenge_to_recovery_sale: A person challenges a property sale conducted to recover a debt in a recovery proceeding.
predicates.unregistered_agreement_claim: The challenger relies on an unregistered agreement to sell as the basis for claiming ownership of the property.
predicates.abandoned_recovery_objection: The challenger filed an objection in the recovery proceeding but stopped pursuing it before the sale was ordered.
predicates.available_appeal_bypassed: A statutory appeal against the Recovery Officer’s order was available, but the challenger did not use it.
predicates.delayed_challenge_after_third_party_righ: The challenger brought the challenge only after the sale had been completed and rights in the property had arisen in a third party.

issues.definition: When a person challenges a recovery sale on the basis of an unregistered agreement after abandoning an objection, bypassing an available appeal, and waiting until third-party rights arise, the belated challenge is rejected.
